body.html: ATP is the universal chemical energy currency of cells. It is made by the same principle everywhere: electron transport builds a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase. It is spent on pumps such as the Na+/K+-ATPase (resting potential, renal reabsorption) and on muscle contraction. The lecture also traces the discoveries and Nobel Prizes behind ATP.

YearWhoWhat
1929Karl LohmannInitial discovery of ATP
1937Herman KalckarATP synthesis is driven by cell respiration
1939-1941Fritz LipmannATP is the universal chemical energy in cells; discovered coenzyme A (Nobel 1953)
1953Hans KrebsCitric acid cycle (Nobel Physiology or Medicine 1953, shared with Lipmann)
1961Efraim RackerFirst isolation of the catalytic F1 subunit of ATP synthase
1978Peter MitchellChemiosmotic mechanism of ATP synthesis
1997Paul Boyer and John Walker; Jens SkouEnzymatic mechanism of ATP synthesis; first ion-transporting enzyme, Na+,K+-ATPase (Nobel Chemistry 1997)

Photosynthesis (plants)Aerobic respiration
H2O → electrons → NADP+: water oxidised, O2 produced, NADPH generatedNADH/FADH2 → electrons → O2: O2 receives electrons, H2O produced
Light energy → chemical energy (photophosphorylation)Chemical energy → ATP

Both rely on electron transport, a proton gradient and ATP synthase. Bacteria (prokaryotes) also make ATP this way, across their plasma membrane.

• Resting potential about −70 mV; threshold about −55 mV; action potential peaks about +40 mV; then repolarisation and refractory period (Hodgkin, Nobel 1963).
  • At rest, all voltage-gated Na+ channels and most voltage-gated K+ channels are closed; the Na+/K+ transporter pumps K+ in and Na+ out.
  • Concentrations: outside Na+ 140 mM, K+ 5 mM; inside Na+ 15 mM, K+ 140 mM.
  • Na+/K+-ATPase: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP (3:2).

• Renal proximal tubule: the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase creates the Na+ gradient used by apical SGLT (glucose) and NHE3 (Na+/H+ exchanger); glucose leaves through GLUT. SGLT2 inhibitors block glucose reabsorption.
  • Cardiac cell: Na+/K+-ATPase (3:2), Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (3:1) and Ca2+-ATPase. Digoxin (from Digitalis lanata) inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase.
The cross-bridge cycle needs ATP: ATP binding detaches myosin from actin, and its hydrolysis re-cocks the myosin head. Lack of ATP leads to rigor mortis: myosin stays locked to actin.

Body weight follows energy balance: intake versus expenditure, around a set point that is 30-50% hereditary. Appetite is controlled by gut-brain peptides: short-term (ghrelin, PYY, CCK) and long-term (leptin, insulin) signals converge on the arcuate nucleus, which has a hunger network (NPY, AgRP) and a satiety network (melanocortins). The lecture opens with two poisons of the electron transport chain: cyanide and DNP.

CyanideDNP (dinitrophenol)
TargetComplex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)H+ gradient / inner mitochondrial membrane
MechanismETC inhibitorUncoupler / protonophore: H+ leaks back into the matrix without passing ATP synthase
Electron transport↓↓ / stops↑
O2 consumption↓↓↑
Proton gradient↓↓
ATP synthesis↓↓↓↓↓
Fuel oxidation↓↑

• Intake = output: stable weight; intake > output: gain; output > intake: loss.
  • Weight has a stable homeostatic set point, varying between people.
  • 30 to 50% of variation in weight is hereditary; environment (eating and exercise habits) accounts for 50 to 70%.

Weight control uses peptide hormones that act as gut-brain signals.

  • Short-term regulators (minutes to hours): make us hungry and start eating, or satiated and stop. Ghrelin (hunger), PYY and CCK (satiety).
  • Long-term regulators (weeks to years): govern calorie intake and expenditure. Leptin, insulin.

HormoneSourceKey points
Ghrelin (hunger)Parietal cells of the gastric fundus, empty stomachSensation of hunger; stimulates the hypothalamus to secrete GH-RH (ghrelin receptor = GHS-R); primes the body for nutrients; secretion stops within an hour of eating
Leptin (satiety)AdipocytesTells the brain how much fat we have; level proportional to fat stores; leptos = thin; gene ob (now LEP); ob/ob mice lack leptin and are obese (Zhang et al., Nature 1994)
Insulin (satiety)Pancreatic beta cellsBrain receptors; like leptin an index of fat stores but a weaker appetite effect; promotes glucose and amino acid uptake, glycogen and fat synthesis
PYY (satiety)Enteroendocrine cells of the ileum and colonSignals satiety and ends eating; released as soon as food reaches the stomach, long before chyme reaches the ileum; in proportion to calories eaten
CCK (satiety)Enteroendocrine cells of the duodenum and jejunumWith PYY, signals stop eating; acts on the brain and vagal sensory fibres; stimulates bile and pancreatic enzyme secretion
GLP-1GutSatiety hormone acting on the arcuate and paraventricular nuclei

The arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus has receptors for all these signals and two neural networks:

  • Hunger (orexigenic): secretes neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP), two potent appetite stimulants. Ghrelin stimulates them; insulin, PYY, CCK and leptin inhibit them.
  • Satiety (anorexigenic): secretes melanocortins (α-MSH from POMC; also CART), which inhibit eating via MC3 and MC4 receptors in the paraventricular nucleus. Leptin stimulates them; AgRP inhibits them.

The median eminence is permeable to the blood-brain barrier, letting these hormones reach the ARC; the sympathetic system links the satiety pathway to energy expenditure.

Metabolism is the sum of all the body's chemical reactions: an energy-balancing act between catabolism (breaking down, releases energy) and anabolism (building up, uses energy). ATP is the molecule that couples them. Nutrients supply the energy and the building blocks; some must come from the diet because the body cannot make them (essential nutrients).

CatabolismAnabolism
WhatBreaks larger molecules into smaller onesBuilds larger molecules from smaller ones
EnergyProvides more than it consumes: exergonicConsumes more than it produces: endergonic
HeatLiberates heat: exothermicAbsorbs heat: endothermic

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the molecule most often used in energy exchanges: it temporarily stores energy from catabolic reactions and transfers it to anabolic reactions. Which reactions occur depends on which enzymes are active in a cell at that time.

A nutrient is any ingested chemical used for growth, repair or maintenance of the body. Nutrients include a necessary chemical (Na+, other minerals), an energy source (lipids, carbohydrates such as glucose), something for growth (vitamins), and something for repair (proteins, amino acids).

Macronutrients (large quantities)Micronutrients (small quantities)
Water, carbohydrates, lipids, proteinsVitamins, minerals

The six essential nutrient classes: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, water, vitamins, minerals.

Essential nutrients cannot be synthesised by the body:

  • Minerals: calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, iron, zinc, iodine, selenium...
  • Most vitamins: A, C, D, E, K, B complex
  • Nine amino acids: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine
  • Fatty acids: linoleic acid (omega-6), alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3)
  • Water must be consumed in the diet
Essential nutrientsRDAs (recommended daily allowances)
A biological conceptA public health guideline
Defines which nutrients are necessaryDefines how much is needed
Same for all humansVaries with age, sex, pregnancy and other factors

The RDA is a safe estimate of daily intake meeting the needs of most healthy people.

• A measure of the capacity to do biological work.
  • One calorie = heat needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C.
  • 1 000 calories = 1 kilocalorie (kcal) in physiology = 1 Calorie in dietetics.
  • Sugar and alcohol (alcohol 7 kcal/g) are 'empty' calories: few nutrients, and they suppress appetite.
  • Good nutrition needs a large variety of foods meeting the needs for essential protein, lipids, vitamins and minerals.

Fat is the body's main energy store: compact, water-free and over twice as energy-rich as carbohydrate. Because triglycerides and cholesterol are hydrophobic, they travel in lipoproteins: chylomicrons from the gut, VLDL and LDL from the liver to the cells, and HDL back to the liver.

• Average body fat: 15% in men, 25% in women.
  • A well-nourished adult meets 80 to 90% of resting energy needs from fat.
  • Fat beats carbohydrate for storage: carbohydrates are hydrophilic (absorb water, expand), fat is hydrophobic and compact; and fat has 9 kcal/g versus 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate.
  • Glucose-sparing (glucose kept for cells such as neurons that cannot use fat) and protein-sparing effects.
  • Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K are absorbed with fat; less than 20 g fat/day risks vitamin deficiency.

• 'Fat' strictly means triglycerides, one subgroup of lipids; others: waxes, sterols (steroid hormones), fat-soluble vitamins, mono- and diglycerides, phospholipids.
  • Triglyceride = glycerol backbone + 3 fatty acids: a condensed form of usable energy.
  • Fatty acids: 4 to 24 carbons; saturated (single C-C bonds) or unsaturated (double or triple bonds).
  • Triglycerides are nonpolar and very hydrophobic, so they travel bound to lipoproteins (made in the liver).

All lipoproteins have a hydrophilic outer shell (polar proteins, amphipathic phospholipids, cholesterol) and a hydrophobic core carrying triglycerides and cholesterol. Classified by density (the slide says higher density = higher lipid content; in fact density rises as the protein share rises):

TypeSizeMain content
Chylomicrons75-1 200 nmTG 90%, cholesterol 5%, phospholipid 3%, protein 2%
VLDL30-80 nmTG 55%, cholesterol 20%, phospholipid 17%, protein 8%
LDL18-25 nmCholesterol 53%, phospholipid 21%, protein 20%, TG 6%
HDL5-12 nmProtein 50%, phospholipid 25%, cholesterol 20%, TG 5%

• Chylomicron pathway: lymph absorbs chylomicrons from the small intestine → drain into the blood → lipoprotein lipase removes lipids → stored in adipocytes or used; the liver disposes of the remnants.
  • VLDL/LDL pathway: liver produces VLDL → triglycerides removed and stored in adipocytes → VLDL becomes LDL (mainly cholesterol) → cells absorb LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis. LDL delivers cholesterol to cells.
  • HDL pathway: the liver makes empty HDL shells → they pick up cholesterol and phospholipids from tissues → return to the liver, which excretes excess cholesterol and bile acids (converts HDL cholesterol into bile salts). HDL removes excess cholesterol.

• High LDL is a warning sign: correlates with cholesterol deposition in arteries; raised by saturated fat, smoking, coffee and stress.
  • High HDL is beneficial: cholesterol is being removed from arteries to the liver.
  • Recommendation: increase the HDL to LDL ratio with regular aerobic exercise, and avoid smoking, saturated fats, coffee and stress.
Fatty acids (triglycerides)Cholesterol
Main roleEnergy source and storageStructural and regulatory
EnergyMajor fuel (9 kcal/g), stored in adiposeNot used for energy
MembranesFlexibility (unsaturated)Rigidity and stability
HormonesPrecursors of eicosanoids (prostaglandins, leukotrienes)Precursor of steroid hormones (oestrogen, testosterone, cortisol)
VitaminsNo direct rolePrecursor of vitamin D

All carbohydrate digestion ends in glucose. Glucose is burnt in small enzyme-controlled steps (cellular respiration: glycolysis, acetyl-CoA, Krebs cycle, electron transport) so its energy goes as much as possible into ATP; the rest is heat. Glucose not needed now is stored as glycogen; when needed, glycogen is broken down, and in fasting new glucose is made (gluconeogenesis).

• Roles: structural cell components, backbone of nucleic acids (ribose and deoxyribose are pentoses), cell signalling, and a major energy source.
  • Formula (CH2O)n, n > 3; glucose n = 6, C6H12O6 (a hexose).
  • Monosaccharides (single sugars, e.g. glucose, galactose, fructose); disaccharides (2); oligosaccharides (3 to 10); polysaccharides (more than 10).
  • The small intestine and liver convert galactose and fructose to glucose: all carbohydrate digestion ultimately gives glucose.
  • Normal blood glucose: 70 to 110 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.1 g/L).
  • Starch, cellulose and glycogen are all polymers of glucose.

Cellulose is non-digestible (humans lack the enzyme): slows digestion, prevents constipation, fills the stomach (less intake), lowers heart disease risk; in oats, nuts, peas, vegetables.

Disaccharidases: sucrase (table sugar), lactase (β-galactosidase; milk), maltase. Without lactase, lactose reaches the large intestine where bacterial fermentation makes gas and acids: nausea, diarrhoea, bloating and gas, abdominal cramps (lactose intolerance). With lactase, lactose → glucose + galactose.

C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O (oxidative carbohydrate metabolism); its function is to transfer energy from glucose to ATP. It runs as a series of small steps, each controlled by its own enzyme, releasing energy in manageable amounts; the rest is lost as heat. Wastes: CO2 and water.

Cellular respiration in 4 steps: 1. glycolysis, 2. formation of acetyl-CoA, 3. Krebs cycle, 4. electron transport chain.

• Ten steps. Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose 6-phosphate (G6P): keeps intracellular glucose low (so glucose keeps diffusing in) and traps it (phosphorylated compounds cannot cross the membrane).
  • G6P can be converted to fat or amino acids, polymerised to glycogen, or oxidised.
  • 4 ATP made but 2 used: net gain 2 ATP per glucose.
  • End products: 2 pyruvic acid + 2 NADH + 2 ATP + 2 H+. Some energy is in ATP, some in NADH, some lost as heat, but most remains in pyruvate.
  • Pyruvate is oxidised to 2 acetyl-CoA, which enter the Krebs cycle.

title: Coenzymes and the electron transport chain
subject: subj:physio

body.html:
Enzymes remove 2 H+ and 2 e− at a time and pass them to coenzymes, which become temporary energy carriers:

  • NAD+ (from niacin, a B vitamin): NAD+ + 2 H → NADH + H+ (binds 2 electrons, 1 proton).
  • FAD (from riboflavin): FAD + 2 H+ + 2 e− → FADH2.

Aerobic respiration: most ATP is made in mitochondria and needs oxygen. Matrix reactions (Krebs) and membrane reactions (electron transport on the cristae). Electrons pass through enzyme complexes (CoQ, cytochromes b, c1, c, a, a3); pumped protons make a gradient that drives ATP synthase (chemiosmosis). Oxygen is the final electron acceptor: each O atom takes 2 e− from cytochrome a3 and 2 H+ → water, the body's main metabolic water. No oxygen: too little ATP to sustain life.

Where: glycolysis in the cytoplasm; Krebs in the mitochondrial matrix; cytochromes in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

ProcessWhat
GlycogenesisGlucose → glycogen (glycogen synthase), the only stored carbohydrate; about 500 g, 75% in skeletal muscle, the rest in the liver
GlycogenolysisGlycogen → glucose (glycogen phosphorylase) when ATP is needed
Gluconeogenesis'New' glucose from non-carbohydrates: lactic acid, amino acids, glycerol; always going, large-scale in fasting, starvation, low-carbohydrate diet

Glucose 6-phosphatase (liver, kidney, intestine) frees glucose into the blood; hexokinase (all cells) traps it. All fuels (triglycerides, polysaccharides, proteins) converge on pyruvate and acetyl-CoA → citric acid cycle → CO2 + H2O + ATP; amino acids leave NH2 as urea.

The revision lecture ties the module to obesity: how it is measured (BMI), how leptin signalling can fail at three points (no leptin, no transport, no receptor), how leptin and insulin talk to each other, and the target values for cholesterol and triglycerides.

• Obesity: weight more than 20% above the recommended norm for age, sex and height.
  • US rates: 30% obese, another 35% overweight.
  • BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)².
  • 20 to 25: optimal for most people; over 25: overweight; above 30: obese.

• Wild type: leptin → satiety → food intake regulation.
  • Ob/ob (ob gene mutation): no leptin → no satiety → always hungry. Human children with this mutation become massively obese and respond to recombinant leptin (Farooqi and O'Rahilly).
  • High leptin with obesity: abnormal leptin receptor (Ob-R).
  • Abnormal transporter for leptin across the blood-brain barrier (endothelium, pericytes, astrocyte end-feet).

Leptin is a long-term regulator; ghrelin a short-term one. Both converge on the hypothalamus (NPY/AgRP hunger vs POMC/α-MSH satiety, MC3/MC4 receptors in the paraventricular nucleus).

• Insulin: from pancreatic beta cells; stimulates glucose and amino acid uptake; promotes glycogen and fat synthesis (inhibits fat breakdown); has brain receptors and, like leptin, indexes fat stores, but its appetite effect is weaker.
  • In healthy people, leptin inhibits insulin biosynthesis and secretion from beta cells.
  • By contrast, insulin stimulates leptin secretion from adipose tissue.
  • Both signal through the hypothalamus (leptin: LepRb, JAK2, STAT3, SOCS3; insulin: IRS, PI3K, AKT, FOXO1) onto POMC and NPY neurons.

LDL delivers cholesterol to cells; HDL removes excess cholesterol (the liver turns it into bile salts).

MeasureValues
Total cholesterolDesirable below 5.0; borderline 5.0-6.2; high above 6.2
HDLToo low below 1.0 (men) / 1.2 (women); satisfactory above 1.6
LDLDesirable below 2.6; normal 2.6-3.3; borderline 3.3-4.1; high 4.1-4.9; excessive above 4.9
TriglyceridesNormal below 1.7; borderline high 1.7-2.3; high 2.3-5.6
Established heart disease or diabetesTotal cholesterol no more than 4.5; LDL no more than 2.5

Neurons talk in two languages. Along the axon the signal is electrical; across the gap between two cells it becomes chemical, because current cannot cross the synaptic cleft. Every neuron-to-neuron message is therefore electrical → chemical → electrical: an action potential in the presynaptic cell, a neurotransmitter crossing the cleft, and a graded (or action) potential in the postsynaptic cell.

The second half of the lecture turns to sensory physiology: how receptors turn stimuli into electrical signals, how the nervous system codes intensity and location, and how responses adapt.

title: What the lecture asks you to do
subject: subj:physio

body.html:
• Describe the structure of a synapse and how information crosses it.
  • Describe neurotransmitter release, including the role of calcium.
  • Compare excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters and give the main examples in the CNS.
  • Describe how neurotransmitter is cleared from the synapse.
  • Explain temporal and spatial summation of synaptic potentials.
  • Outline the differences between chemical and electrical synapses.

title: The special senses at a glance
subject: subj:physio

body.html:
SenseReceptorsPathway
SmellOlfactory receptors in the olfactory epitheliumOlfactory bulb, CN I, limbic system and hypothalamus, olfactory cortex
TasteGustatory receptors in taste budsCN VII, IX, X → medulla → thalamus → gustatory cortex
HearingHair cells of the cochleaCN VIII → medullary olives, inferior colliculus → thalamus → auditory cortex
BalanceHair cells of the semicircular canals and vestibuleCN VIII → vestibular nuclei (pons, medulla), cerebellum, cortex
VisionPhotoreceptorsOptic nerve, chiasm (some fibres cross), optic tract → thalamus → visual cortex; also hypothalamus, superior colliculus, pineal gland (day/night)

A synapse is a connection point between a neuron and another neuron, a muscle (neuromuscular synapse), a gland (neuroglandular synapse) or another cell.

PartWhat it holds
Presynaptic neuron (sends the signal)Axon terminal with synaptic vesicles full of neurotransmitter, and voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in its membrane
Synaptic cleftThe space between terminal and postsynaptic cell: electrical signals cannot pass, chemicals can
Postsynaptic cell (receives the signal)Neurotransmitter receptors and ion channels in its membrane

Chemical versus electrical synapses (standard comparison): electrical synapses join cells through gap junctions, are almost instantaneous and can pass current both ways; chemical synapses are one-way, have a short synaptic delay, and can amplify, inhibit and be modulated, which is why most CNS synapses are chemical.

1. Action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal (purely electrical conduction).
  2. Ca²⁺ entry: voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ enters the terminal.
  3. Neurotransmitter release: Ca²⁺ triggers exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
  4. Receptor activation: the transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors.
  5. Ions enter: receptor binding opens ion channels in the postsynaptic membrane.
  6. Graded potential at the postsynaptic dendrite, which can lead to an action potential.

Steps 1 to 3 are presynaptic; 4 to 6 are postsynaptic. Calcium is the link between the electrical and the chemical step: block the Ca²⁺ channels and release stops even though the action potential arrives normally.

The graded potential caused by a synapse is a postsynaptic potential (PSP).

EPSPIPSP
IonsPositive ions in (e.g. Na⁺)Negative ions in (e.g. Cl⁻)
EffectDepolarizes, towards thresholdHyperpolarizes, away from threshold
ResultCan lead to action potentialsReduces the number of action potentials

Which channel opens depends on both the transmitter and the receptor type. Numbers to know: resting potential -70 mV, threshold -50 to -55 mV, each PSP about ±10 mV. So a single EPSP cannot fire an action potential; EPSPs must add up. The axon hillock keeps score of all the graded potentials arriving at the dendrites.

  • Temporal summation: one presynaptic neuron fires repeatedly in quick succession at the same location, so its EPSPs stack up in time.
  • Spatial summation: several presynaptic neurons stimulate the postsynaptic cell at the same time at different locations.
  • An EPSP and an IPSP arriving together can cancel each other out.

Convergence: one cell is influenced by many others (thousands of inputs). Divergence: one cell branches to influence many others.

In general one neuron releases one type of transmitter, but any neuron can respond to several.

TransmitterWhere / role
AcetylcholineNeuromuscular junctions, autonomic nervous system
GlutamateThe main excitatory transmitter in the brain
GABAThe main inhibitory transmitter in the brain (glycine is also inhibitory)
NoradrenalineAutonomic nervous system; learning, emotion, behaviour
Dopamine, serotoninLearning, emotion, behavioural pathways

By chemical structure: acetylcholine; biogenic amines (catecholamines, serotonin); amino acids (glutamate, glycine, GABA); peptides (endorphins, substance P); other messengers (ATP, dissolved gases such as NO).

By function: excitatory (glutamate) or inhibitory (GABA, glycine). Some transmitters can be both, depending on the receptor: acetylcholine is excitatory at the neuromuscular junction (nicotinic receptor) and inhibitory in cardiac muscle (muscarinic receptor).

Receptor mechanisms:

  • Direct (the receptor is an ion channel): rapid responses, fast synapses. Examples: ACh, amino acids.
  • Indirect (second messengers): G protein → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → enzyme activation, changes in permeability, gene expression. Long-lasting, slow synapses. Examples: biogenic amines, peptides, dissolved gases.

The effect on the membrane depends on how much transmitter is released and how long it stays bound.

title: Ending the signal, drugs and disease
subject: subj:physio

body.html:
A graded potential lasts as long as the transmitter is bound, so it must be removed:

  1. Active transport (reuptake) back into the presynaptic terminal or into nearby glia.
  2. Enzymes in the cleft break it down, e.g. acetylcholinesterase.
  3. Diffusion away from the cleft.

Acetylcholine: AChE splits ACh into acetate + choline; choline is actively taken back into the terminal and ChAT (choline acetyltransferase) rebuilds ACh from choline + acetyl CoA.

Drugs can alter synthesis, storage or release, the transmitter-receptor interaction, reuptake or destruction, or replace a missing transmitter. Lecture examples: SSRIs block serotonin reuptake, keeping serotonin longer in the synapse (depression). Tetanus toxin prevents GABA release from inhibitory neurons, causing uncontrolled spasms and lockjaw (too much excitation).

Perception is the conscious interpretation of the world, created by patterns of brain activity; it is limited by our receptor types (we do not sense magnetic fields or UV), our sensitivity (only certain sound frequencies) and central filtering (attention). The cerebral cortex handles both sensation (awareness of the stimulus) and perception (its interpretation).

The afferent division carries information to the CNS: somatic afferents (skin, skeletal muscle, joints), special sense afferents (eye, ear, taste, smell) and visceral afferents (organs of the body cavities, not consciously perceived).

A receptor is either (1) the specialised ending of the afferent neuron itself or (2) a separate receptor cell that releases transmitter onto the afferent neuron. Transduction converts stimulus energy (light, heat, sound) into electrical energy: the receptor potential, a depolarizing graded potential with no refractory period that can summate. Its trigger zone is on the dendrite, not the axon hillock.

Receptor types: photoreceptors (light), mechanoreceptors (stretch, touch, sound, blood pressure), thermoreceptors, osmoreceptors (solute concentration), chemoreceptors (taste, smell) and nociceptors (tissue damage). Each receptor has an adequate stimulus but may respond weakly to others: pressing on the eye makes you 'see' light.

Intensity is coded by the number of receptors stimulated and the frequency of action potentials (a stronger stimulus gives a larger receptor potential and more action potentials per second).

Tonic receptorsPhasic receptors
AdaptationSlow or noneRapid
FiringContinuous while the stimulus lastsBursts at the start (and end) of the stimulus
UseMaintenance information: posture, balanceSignalling change
ExamplesProprioceptors, muscle stretch receptorsTouch (a ring or watch is soon not felt), temperature, smell
  • Receptor adaptation: less depolarization to a sustained or repeated stimulus, so fewer action potentials (a smell 'goes away').
  • Habituation: neurons reduce their response to repeated stimuli by depressing synaptic activity, e.g. through changes in presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.
  • Sensitization: a strong or noxious stimulus increases responsiveness. Mechanism: serotonin → cAMP cascade → K⁺ channels blocked → presynaptic action potential prolonged → more Ca²⁺ enters → more transmitter released.

• First-order neuron: from the receptor to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord or the medullary nuclei.
  • Second-order neuron: in the spinal cord or medulla; crosses to the other side and projects to the thalamus.
  • Third-order neuron: from the thalamus to the cortex, where sensations are perceived in the primary somatic sensory cortex.

Where they cross: pain, temperature and coarse touch cross in the spinal cord; fine touch, vibration and proprioception cross in the medulla. So a cord lesion on one side removes pain and temperature on the opposite side below it.

Labeled lines: information of one type from one place travels together and builds sensory 'maps' in the CNS. The cortical area given to a region matches its sensitivity (the sensory homunculus). Receptive fields: small and dense in sensitive areas (fingertips: two points felt as two), large in less sensitive ones (lower leg: two points felt as one). Lateral inhibition sharpens contrast: the field nearest the stimulus is most active and its neighbours are suppressed.

OrganSympatheticParasympathetic
PupilDilatedConstricted
SalivaSlightCopious
GutLess motileMore motile
Bladder sphincterContractedRelaxed
HeartFaster, strongerSlower
BronchiDilatedConstricted
Skin vesselsConstrictedNone

Transmitters: ACh at all autonomic ganglia (nicotinic) and all parasympathetic terminals (muscarinic); NE at most sympathetic terminals (alpha or beta). Smooth muscle responds to muscarine, skeletal muscle to nicotine.

Three sympathetic exceptions: sweat glands release ACh; renal vessels receive dopamine; the adrenal medulla is supplied directly by preganglionic fibres and releases adrenaline and noradrenaline 4:1.

Without at least one peripheral synapse, the CNS has no direct control of smooth muscle and glands, whereas it drives skeletal muscle directly at the neuromuscular junction.

This lecture is the map of the whole module: how the nervous system is organised, how CSF protects it, how the autonomic system talks to organs, and how sensation, including pain, gets in. Each later lecture zooms into one part of this map.

31 pairs of spinal nerves leave through the intervertebral foramina and join into plexuses. White matter forms posterior, anterior and lateral funiculi. Medial local circuit neurons control posture; lateral ones the fine control of distal limbs.

PathwayTractsCarries
Direct motorLateral and anterior corticospinal, corticobulbarVoluntary movement
Indirect motorRubrospinal, tectospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinalAutomatic movement, tone
SpinothalamicAnterolateralPain, temperature, itch, crude touch
Posterior columnGracile and cuneateDiscriminative touch, vibration, conscious proprioception

A dermatome is skin mapping to one spinal level; a myotome the muscles of one level. Cord section causes paralysis and sensory loss below the lesion.

CSF is made by the choroid plexus and flows: lateral ventricles, foramen of Monro, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, foramen of Magendie, subarachnoid space, arachnoid granulations, superior sagittal sinus.

The meninges are dura, arachnoid and pia; where the pia follows the brain's folds and the arachnoid does not, cisterns of CSF form.

Functions of CSF: protection, buoyancy (1400 g to about 50 g), excretion of waste and an endocrine medium. Hydrocephalus is abnormal CSF build-up in the ventricles, raising intracranial pressure.

Neurophysiology studies the function of neurons, glia and networks, historically by electrophysiology (EEG to single-cell recording) and now also by calcium imaging, fMRI and molecular biology.

PartComponentsRole
CNSBrain and spinal cordThe control centre
PNSNerves, ganglia, sensory organsCarries signals in and out
SomaticSkeletal muscleVoluntary
AutonomicSmooth and cardiac muscle, glandsInvoluntary: sympathetic and parasympathetic
EntericGut plexusesThe brain of the gut

Functions: sensory input, integration, motor output. The lobes are divided by the central sulcus, the lateral (Sylvian) fissure and the parieto-occipital sulcus.

Pain: nociceptors are specialised, with a threshold near 45°C. First pain (sharp) travels in A-delta fibres, second pain (burning) in C fibres. C fibres end in Rexed laminae 1 and 2, A-delta in 1 and 5; second-order axons cross and ascend in the anterolateral system, serving both the sensory-discriminative and the affective-motivational aspects of pain.

Sensitisation: peripheral (the inflammatory soup) and central (dorsal horn excitability). Gate theory: A-beta touch input and descending enkephalin neurons inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.

Muscle turns chemical energy (ATP) into force. This lecture builds the machine: three muscle types, the layers from whole muscle down to the sarcomere, the proteins that make the filaments, and the sliding filament idea that explains contraction. Part II (on the site) then follows the signal from nerve to muscle and looks at force, energy, fatigue and disease.

One rule to keep: muscle can only pull. It produces force by shortening, never by pushing or lengthening.

SkeletalSmoothCardiac
WhereAttached to bonesWalls of hollow organs, vessels, eye, glands, skinHeart only
NucleiMany, peripheralOne, centralOne, central

Skeletal fibres form when 100 or more myoblasts (mesodermal cells) fuse during development.

• Contractility: shortens with force as filaments slide; it does not produce force by lengthening or pushing.
  • Conductivity: propagates action potentials along the sarcolemma, like an axon.
  • Excitability: responds to a stimulus (neurotransmitter) by changing membrane potential.
  • Extensibility: can be stretched.
  • Elasticity: recoils to resting length.

Functions: movement (bones, speech, breathing, swallowing), posture and joint stability, respiration, heat production, holding organs in place, controlling flow through organs and vessels, and the heartbeat. A little less than half of body mass is skeletal muscle.

TermMeaning
Muscle fibreOne muscle cell (multinucleate)
SarcolemmaPlasma membrane; a change in its potential starts contraction
SarcoplasmCytoplasm
Sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)Endoplasmic reticulum around each myofibril; its terminal cisternae concentrate Ca²⁺ with pumps and release it to start contraction
T-tubulesInfoldings of the sarcolemma that carry the action potential deep into the fibre, so the whole fibre contracts at once
TriadOne T-tubule + two terminal cisternae
MyofibrilsLengthwise bundles of myofilaments: thin (actin) and thick (myosin)

The number of fibres is fixed at birth: training enlarges fibres (hypertrophy), it does not add new ones. A fibre can hold about 100,000 sarcomeres end to end.

• Contractile: actin and myosin, which produce movement.
  • Regulatory: tropomyosin and troponin, which control contraction through Ca²⁺ binding.
  • Structural: titin (spans half a sarcomere; structural, signalling and mechanical roles), nebulin, CapZ.

The body has three motor proteins: myosin (with actin: all muscle contraction), kinesins (walk organelles along microtubules) and dyneins (bend cilia and flagella).

Myosin is a hexamer: 2 heavy chains + 4 light chains. The head (S1 fragment) holds all the motor function: an N-terminal catalytic domain with the nucleotide (ATP) binding site and the actin-binding site. The neck acts as a lever arm: small changes at the ATP site swing it to move the end 5 to 10 nm, the power stroke. The tails coil together (two α-helices) and pack into the thick filament. Myosin II is a plus-end actin motor.

RegionName meansContains
Z disc'Zwischen', betweenBoundary between sarcomeres; thin filaments anchored here (CapZ)

A bandAnisotropic (dark)The full length of the thick filaments (with overlapping thin ones)

Filaments are 1 to 2 µm long; thin filaments about 8 nm wide, thick about 16 nm; about 2 thin filaments per thick filament. The overlap pattern creates the striations.

Membrane proteins: sarcolemma: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (propagate APs), the DHP receptor (a voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel in the T-tubule) and the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase. SR: ryanodine receptors (Ca²⁺ channels gated by the DHP receptors) and the SR Ca²⁺ ATPase (SERCA, removes Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasm).

title: Sliding filaments and types of contraction
subject: subj:physio

body.html:
• Thin (actin) filaments slide over thick (myosin) filaments towards the M line, shortening the sarcomere from Z disc to Z disc.
  • Actin and myosin do not change length. The A band stays the same; the I band and H zone shorten (and can disappear at full contraction).
  • ATP hydrolysis powers the myosin head to detach and re-cock; each cycle pulls actin a step.
  • During relaxation sarcomeres lengthen again.
  • Elastic components (titin, endomysium, perimysium, epimysium, tendons) stretch first and then transfer the tension to the bone.

Isotonic contraction: the muscle shortens (load moves). Isometric contraction: myosin heads rotate and generate tension, but the thin filaments cannot slide because the opposing load is too great, so the muscle does not shorten.

Smooth muscle has no sarcomeres, which is one reason it is slow; excitation-contraction coupling is mechanical in skeletal muscle and chemical (second messengers) in smooth muscle.

Muscle contraction is a relay. The nerve releases ACh, the end plate depolarizes, the action potential runs down the T-tubules, the sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca2+, Ca2+ binds troponin, and myosin grabs actin.

Most diseases in this lecture break one link: myasthenia at the receptor, Lambert-Eaton at the Ca2+ channel, McArdle at the energy supply, Duchenne in the fibre's structure.

The glycogen storage myopathies are autosomal recessive. In dystrophy, nNOS falls off its dystrophin scaffold, so the lack of nitric oxide causes vasoconstriction, ischaemia and further degeneration. Gene therapy, exon skipping and CRISPR repair are being studied.

1. Action potentials propagate along the T-tubules.
  2. L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, the DHP receptors, open.
  3. They trigger the ryanodine receptors of the SR to release Ca2+.
  4. Ca2+ binds troponin, unmasking the myosin sites on actin.
  5. SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the SR.

Resting cytosolic Ca2+ is about 0.1 µmol/L; the SR holds up to 10,000 times more, and release raises cytosolic Ca2+ tenfold or more. A single action potential gives a twitch; several summate.

All fibres in a motor unit are the same type, and fibre type is set by motor neuron activity. Muscle is plastic: endurance training (15 to 20 percent of maximal force) adds mitochondria, myoglobin, capillaries and GLUT4 with little hypertrophy; strength training (75 to 90 percent) causes hypertrophy. Disuse causes atrophy, mostly of type II fibres, reversible in the young.

Fatigue is the inability to maintain the desired output, when ATP use outpaces synthesis: low pH from lactate, low glycogen, depleted reserves, damage to the sarcolemma and SR. Types: psychological, muscular and synaptic. Fats burn in the flame of carbohydrates: glucose supplies the oxaloacetate the TCA cycle needs to burn fatty acids, so glycogen depletion makes endurance athletes hit the wall.

Fatigue versus rigor mortis: fatigue occurs at about 30 percent ATP depletion; rigor mortis is complete depletion, so cross-bridges cannot detach; it starts about 3 hours after death and lasts up to 72 hours.

The sarcoplasm holds ATP for only about 8 twitches; the creatine kinase shunt keeps ADP/ATP low, backed by glycolysis and oxidative metabolism.

Single-fibre tension depends on the number of pivoting cross-bridges, the resting length and the stimulation frequency. Optimal filament overlap gives maximum tension; resting sarcomere length is 75 to 130 percent of optimal.

Whole-muscle force is graded by recruiting motor units (the most important means) and by raising frequency. Fewer fibres per unit means finer movement.

Twitch and summation. A twitch has lag, contraction and relaxation phases. Rising frequency gives incomplete tetanus, then fused tetanus. Treppe: in a rested muscle each contraction is stronger than the last. Isotonic contractions shorten the muscle; isometric contractions develop tension without shortening.

A motor unit is one motor neuron and all the fibres it supplies, contracting together; each fibre has only one neuron.

The NMJ is a chemical synapse. Vesicles hold about 1000 ACh molecules each; the cleft is about 50 nm, crossed in about 0.5 ms; the motor end plate carries nicotinic receptors in junctional folds.

  1. A neuronal action potential.
  2. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open.
  3. ACh is released.
  4. ACh diffuses and binds its receptor.
  5. The cation pore opens and Na+ enters.
  6. An end plate potential (EPP) develops.
  7. AChE splits ACh into choline and acetate; choline is taken back up.

The nicotinic receptor is a ligand-gated cation channel; two ACh bind its two α subunits. AChE is unregulated, so longer stimulation needs more ACh.

From mEPP to action potential. One vesicle gives about 0.5 mV (an mEPP). About 100 vesicles sum to an EPP of about 50 mV, which brings nearby membrane to threshold.

Tap a tendon and the muscle jerks, without the brain being involved. That is the myotatic (stretch) reflex: the muscle spindle senses the stretch, a Ia fibre carries it to the cord, and one synapse later an alpha motor neuron contracts the same muscle.

Clinically this is gold: a reflex that is too weak points to the arc itself, and one that is too brisk points to a lesion above it.

ReflexMuscleResponse

TricipitalTricepsForearm extension
GradeResponse

H-reflex (Hoffmann). A stimulus at the popliteal fossa first travels down motor fibres to the soleus (the M wave), then up the Ia fibres to the motor neuron and back, recorded later as the H-reflex. An EMG comparing the Achilles reflex with a voluntary contraction shows the spinal cord is the reflex centre.

Monosynaptic, triggered by sudden passive stretch of the muscle belly: the agonist contracts while the antagonist relaxes.

  • Tonic phase: maintains upright posture. The anti-gravity extensors are stretched as the body flexes and contract reflexly, creating tone. The weight of the head stretches the neck extensors, which respond by contracting. In the waiter example, water added to a tray stretches the biceps and the reflex keeps the tray steady.
  • Phasic phase: a sudden change in length, such as a tendon tap, triggers a brief contraction through Ia afferents, preventing overstretch.

Roles: maintaining tone, maintaining posture, adjusting muscle function during exercise, and preventing injury from overstretching.

Homeostatic imbalance. Reflex changes often precede other signs of disease. Hyporeflexia points to the two-neuron arc; hyperreflexia (brisk or clonic) points to a suprasegmental lesion of the descending pathways.

ReflexTypeMechanism
Stretch (myotatic)MonosynapticSpindle stretch; the same muscle contracts, antagonists relax
TendonPolysynapticTendon organ detects tension; the muscle relaxes and the antagonist contracts

Patellar reflex: centre L2 to L4; often absent in chronic diabetes or neurosyphilis; exaggerated with descending motor tract disease.

Achilles reflex: gastrocnemius and soleus; absent with lumbosacral damage, diabetes, neurosyphilis, alcoholism or subarachnoid haemorrhage; exaggerated with cervical cord compression or an S1 to S2 motor tract lesion.

Babinski sign: stroking the lateral sole extends the great toe. Normal under 1.5 years, before the corticospinal tract is myelinated; after that it indicates a corticospinal lesion.

Cord section causes monoplegia, diplegia, paraplegia, hemiplegia or tetraplegia, with sensory loss below the lesion.

Motor activityFeatures
ReflexElementary, innate, species-specific, involuntary; a stereotyped response to a specific stimulus
Automatic activityInnate but under the will, adaptable, mostly rhythmic: breathing, walking, chewing
Deliberate motricityBased on habits and programmes; always modulated by the cortex and subcortical structures

A reflex is an involuntary, stereotyped response to a specific stimulus. The stimulus's location fixes which muscle contracts; its strength sets the amplitude, so reflexes are graded.

Autonomic reflexesSomatic reflexes
Started byThe visceraSomatic sensory endings
EffectorSoft tissue organsSkeletal muscle
ExamplesGut and reproductive contractions, pupil dilation, defecation, vomitingProtection from injury

Proprioception is the perception of the body in movement and position. Receptors: the spindle (length), the Golgi tendon organ (tension, via group Ib afferents), joint receptors and the vestibular apparatus.

The spindle is a fusiform receptor lying in parallel with the muscle: contraction unloads it, stretch stimulates it. It holds four to eight intrafusal fibres, multinucleated, with contractile poles and a non-contractile centre. Three types: nuclear chain, static nuclear bag and dynamic nuclear bag fibres.

AfferentSize and speedInnervatesSignals
Ia (primary)17 µm, 70 to 110 m/sBag and chain fibres at the equatorLength and speed: velocity and direction of movement
II (secondary)8 µm, 30 to 70 m/sMainly chain fibresLength only: static position

Pathway. T-shaped afferents from the spindle, with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion, synapse in the cord on motor neurons of the same muscle, whose cell bodies lie in the ventral horn. Two synapses: neuron to neuron, and the neuromuscular junction.

Reciprocal inhibition. An inhibitory interneuron relaxes the antagonist: in a knee jerk the quadriceps contracts and the hamstrings relax.

Gamma motor neurons contract the spindle ends to keep it sensitive. In alpha-gamma coactivation both fire together, so the spindle stays taut during contraction. Through gamma output the brain sets spindle sensitivity and overall tone, raising it for demanding movements such as balancing on a beam.

A neuron is a charged battery. At rest the inside sits at about -70 mV. A signal is simply a change in that voltage: small and local (a graded potential) or large and travelling (an action potential).

The action potential is two ions taking turns: Na+ rushes in to depolarize, then K+ flows out to repolarize.

title: Nervous system cells and the neuron
subject: subj:physio

body.html:
Two categories: neurons, the signalling cells, and neuroglia (ependymal cells, astrocytes, Schwann cells, oligodendrocytes, microglia), which support them. The CNS contains over 100 billion neurons and 50 to 100 times as many glia.

ZonePartRole
InputDendrites and cell bodyReceive incoming signals
TriggerAxon hillockInitiates action potentials
ConductingAxon (1 mm to over 1 m)Conducts action potentials without decrement
OutputAxon terminalsRelease neurotransmitter

Unlike other cells, neurons have processes, Nissl granules and neurofibrillae, no centrosome (so they cannot divide), and they secrete neurotransmitters. Every neuron has exactly one axon; dendrites may be absent, one or many.

PartKey facts
Cell body (soma, perikaryon)Nucleus with prominent nucleoli, no centrosome; Nissl granules; neurofibrillae; mitochondria; Golgi apparatus. No process survives without it
Nissl granulesTigroid, basophilic; in the cell body and dendrites, absent from the axon and axon hillock
DendritesConduct toward the soma; generate local, not action, potentials; spines in the cerebral and cerebellar cortex
AxonOne per neuron, from the axon hillock; carries impulses away; cannot make protein; branches only at its terminals; converts electrical to chemical signals
Axis cylinderAxoplasm plus axolemma; covered by neurilemma or by myelin

Classification: by number of poles; by function (motor with a long axon, sensory with long dendrites); by axon length (Golgi type I long, type II short). Synapses join neuron to neuron, neuron to muscle (neuromuscular junction) and neuron to gland.

Neurons communicate electrically, by ions crossing membranes, and chemically, by neurotransmitters at synapses. Stimuli may be mechanical, electrical or chemical.

ChannelOpens when
Mechanically gatedA physical force acts on it
Voltage-gatedThe membrane potential changes
Ligand-gatedA chemical or neurotransmitter binds
Phosphorylation-gatedA phosphate group is attached
LeakAlways open, non-gated

Properties. Channels are transmembrane protein pores; flux through them is always passive, up to a million ions per second. Opening is a conformational change. They are selective by charge (a positive charge in the pore repels cations and passes anions) and by size.

Two factors set how fast an action potential travels:

  1. Myelination. Myelin, from oligodendrocytes (CNS) or Schwann cells (PNS), is up to 300 layers thick, with no channels beneath it. The gaps, the nodes of Ranvier, hold the voltage-gated channels, so the signal jumps node to node: saltatory conduction, faster and needing fewer Na+/K+ pumps.
  2. Axon diameter. Larger means lower resistance. Large axons reach 120 m/s (neuron to skeletal muscle); small ones only 0.7 m/s (neuron to gut).

Space is limited, so an axon that must be fast is both large and myelinated.

Membrane potential is the charge inside compared with outside, in millivolts. Charges line up right at the membrane and cannot cross the lipid bilayer without channels.

A resting neuron sits at -70 mV, because of negative proteins inside, moderate K+ inside and high Na+ outside.

IonConcentration gradientElectrical gradientEquilibrium
K+ (inside)Pushes it outNegative interior holds it inAbout -90 mV
Na+ (outside)Pulls it inNegative interior pulls it inAbout +60 mV

At rest, K+ leak channels are open, so K+ permeability is high and the potential sits near the K+ equilibrium; few Na+ channels are open.

Terms: depolarization (less negative), hyperpolarization (more negative), repolarization (back to rest), threshold (the level that triggers an action potential).

title: What the lecture asks you to do
subject: subj:physio

body.html:
• Know the terminology of changes in membrane potential.
  • Know the neuron's membrane domains, the channels in each and how their opening affects the membrane potential.
  • Know the ionic basis of an action potential: its requirements, which channels shape each phase, what inactivation is and why it matters, and how positive feedback builds it.
  • Know which cells are excitable and why, and why action potentials differ between them.

Graded potentialAction potential
SizeSmall, proportional to the stimulus (V = IR)Large, all or none, always the same
SpreadLocal, fades with distanceLong distance, without decrement
WhereAny membraneMembranes with voltage-gated channels
TypeExcitatory (positive in) or inhibitory (negative in, positive out)Depolarizing, one-way toward the terminal

Graded potentials can summate over time or space. If they reach threshold where voltage-gated channels exist, an action potential fires.

Phases of the action potential

  1. Rest at -70 mV: leak K+ channels open, voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels closed.
  2. Threshold reached at about -50 to -55 mV.
  3. Rising phase: voltage-gated Na+ channels open rapidly and Na+ rushes in.
  4. Falling phase: Na+ channels inactivate; slow K+ channels let K+ out.
  5. Dip: K+ channels close slowly, giving afterhyperpolarization.
  6. Return to rest.

Na+ channels are closed at rest, open rapidly at threshold and are shut by a separate inactivation gate. K+ channels open and close slowly.

Propagation. Starting at the axon hillock, entering Na+ brings the next patch to threshold, a domino effect. The action potential travels only toward the terminal because the Na+ channels behind it are inactivated.

Pain has two lanes. Fast pain travels in A-delta fibres, is sharp and well localised, and warns you to pull away. Slow pain travels in C fibres, burns and aches, and drives suffering. The body can also turn pain down, through the gate in the dorsal horn and the descending analgesia system.

TermMeaning
PainAn unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage
NociceptionUnconscious activity induced by a noxious stimulus
HyperalgesiaAn exaggerated response to a noxious stimulus
AllodyniaPain from a harmless stimulus, such as touch on sunburned skin

Pain is protective: someone who loses it after spinal cord injury no longer shifts weight when sitting and develops pressure damage.

Fast painSlow pain
OnsetWithin 0.1 sAfter 1 s or more, builds
QualitySharp, pricking, electricBurning, aching, throbbing, nauseous
WhereSkin onlySkin and almost any deep tissue
FibreA-delta, 6 to 30 m/sC, 0.5 to 2 m/s
StimuliMechanical and thermalMostly chemical
TransmitterGlutamateGlutamate and substance P

Analgesia system: periaqueductal and periventricular grey, then the raphe magnus, then a pain-inhibitory complex in the dorsal horn. Transmitters: enkephalin and serotonin (which makes local neurons release enkephalin). The PAG holds endorphin neurons and responds to opioids.

Enkephalin reduces presynaptic Ca2+ entry and transmitter release, and opens K+ channels to hyperpolarise the second-order neuron, shrinking its EPSP.

Gate theory: A-beta touch fibres activate inhibitory interneurons that block C-fibre transmission, which is why rubbing the skin, liniments and TENS help.

Entering fibres run 1 to 2 segments in Lissauer's tract. C fibres synapse in laminae 1 and 2, A-delta in 1 and 5; second-order axons cross and ascend in the anterolateral column.

Neospinothalamic (fast)Paleospinothalamic (slow)
FibresA-deltaC
Dorsal hornLamina ILaminae II and III (substantia gelatinosa)
EndsMostly ventrobasal thalamus, then somatosensory cortexReticular nuclei, tectum, PAG; only a tenth to a quarter reach the thalamus
LocalisationPrecisePoor, to a whole limb

Parallel pathways: the discriminative aspect goes via VPL thalamus to S1 and S2; the affective-motivational aspect via the reticular formation, PAG, hypothalamus, amygdala and midline thalamus to the anterior cingulate and insular cortex.

All pain receptors are free nerve endings, dense in the skin, periosteum, arterial walls, joint surfaces and the falx and tentorium. They respond to mechanical, thermal and chemical stimuli and adapt very little.

ReceptorThresholdFibreCapsaicin
TRPV1About 45°CC and A-deltaYes
TRPV2About 52°CA-deltaNo

Chemical exciters: bradykinin (possibly the most painful), serotonin, histamine, K+, acids, ACh, proteolytic enzymes. Sensitisers only: prostaglandins and substance P. In injury, cells release K+, substance P, bradykinin and PGE2; nociceptor terminals release substance P and CGRP; immune cells add IL-1β, growth factors, ATP and H+.

Ischaemia hurts within 15 to 20 s in an exercised ischaemic muscle, versus 3 to 4 minutes at rest (lactic acid, bradykinin, enzymes). Spasm hurts by direct stimulation and by causing ischaemia.

Pain physiology has three components: transduction, transmission and modulation.

Visceral pain comes from ischaemia, chemical damage, spasm, distension or stretching; it travels in C fibres, is poorly localised and comes with nausea, sweating and blood pressure changes. The liver parenchyma, lung alveoli and brain are almost insensitive.

Referred pain: visceral fibres share second-order neurons with skin fibres, so the pain is felt on the skin (convergence-projection). It may be the only sign of visceral disease.

Neuropathic pain arises from direct nerve injury and often persists, unlike nociceptive pain; it is treated with NMDA receptor inhibitors and GABA analogues. Phantom pain is thought to reflect reorganisation of the somatosensory cortex after amputation.

Arterial blood pH is kept between 7.35 and 7.45 (7.40). Three lines of defence: chemical buffers (mainly bicarbonate, act fast), the lungs (CO2) and the kidneys (H+ and HCO3−, slowest but the only way to eliminate acids other than carbonic acid). The kidneys secrete H+, so urine is acidic, and every H+ secreted goes with an HCO3− reabsorbed: urine acidification = blood alkalinisation.

pH = −log [H+]; blood pH is about 7.40. Metabolic reactions produce a huge excess of H+; if homeostatic mechanisms failed, pH would quickly fall to a lethal level.

Acidosis causes hyperkalaemia by shifting K+ from the intracellular to the extracellular space.

• A buffer is effective when pH changes little even when large amounts of acid or base are added.
  • Buffers act quickly to temporarily bind excess H+ or OH−, until they can be permanently excreted.
  • Bicarbonate is the most important extracellular buffer.

pH = 6.1 + log ([HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2)): the numerator (HCO3−) is regulated by the kidneys, the denominator (PCO2) by the respiratory system. Raising alveolar ventilation raises pH; lowering it lowers pH, and arterial pH in turn changes alveolar ventilation.

CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−: lungs act on the CO2 side, kidneys on the H+/HCO3− side.

• Kidney excretion or reabsorption of acidic ions (H+, NH4+) or basic ions (HCO3−, OH−) is the slowest mechanism, but the only way to eliminate acids other than carbonic acid.
  • Kidneys maintain blood pH by secreting H+, so urine is acidic; H+ secretion goes with HCO3− reabsorption.
  • In the proximal tubule, H+ is secreted in exchange for Na+ (secondary active transport driven by the basal Na+–K+ pump, which uses ATP).

1. HCO3− cannot cross the tubule membrane.
  2. It is converted to CO2 and H2O by carbonic anhydrase (H+ secreted + filtered HCO3− → H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O).
  3. CO2 crosses into the tubule cell, where the reaction reverses and HCO3− is made again.
  4. HCO3− diffuses into the interstitial space (with Na+).

Filtered load about 4 320 mEq/day: about 85% reabsorbed in the proximal tubule (3 672 mEq/day), 10% in the thick ascending limb (432), 4.9% in the distal tubule and collecting duct (215); about 1 mEq/day is excreted.

Distal convoluted tubule: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → HCO3− (reabsorbed) + H+ (secreted by the H+-ATPase). For each H+ secreted, one HCO3− is reabsorbed.

1. Nephrons cannot produce urine below pH 4.5.
  2. To secrete more H+, urine must be buffered by phosphates (enter by filtration) and ammonia (from the deamination of amino acids).

GFR is controlled by adjusting glomerular blood pressure from moment to moment, through three mechanisms: renal autoregulation, nervous (sympathetic) control and hormonal control. Autoregulation keeps GFR stable when systemic pressure changes; hormones (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, ANP) adjust volume and pressure.

The ability of nephrons to adjust their own blood flow and GFR without external (nervous or hormonal) control, keeping GFR relatively stable despite changes in systemic blood pressure. Two methods:

  1. Myogenic mechanism (intrinsic autoregulation)
  2. Tubuloglomerular feedback (extrinsic autoregulation)

Based on the tendency of smooth muscle to contract when stretched, to keep capillary flow constant whatever the arterial pressure.

  • Pressure rises → afferent arteriole is stretched → it constricts → flow into the glomerulus does not change.
  • Pressure falls → afferent arteriole dilates → blood flows more easily into the glomerulus → flow and filtration stay stable.

Found where the end of the nephron loop (distal convoluted tubule) has re-entered the cortex and touches the afferent and efferent arterioles at the vascular pole.

  • Macula densa: patch of tall, slender, closely spaced sensory cells in the nephron loop; chemoreceptors for NaCl in the filtrate.
  • Granular (juxtaglomerular) cells: modified smooth muscle cells wrapping the arterioles; contain renin granules; mechanoreceptors sensing blood pressure in the afferent arteriole.
  • Mesangial cells may also contract, constricting capillaries and further limiting GFR.

When GFR is high, filtrate contains more NaCl:

  1. Macula densa cells sense the NaCl.
  2. They secrete ATP in response to increased NaCl absorption.
  3. ATP is metabolised by nearby mesangial cells into adenosine.
  4. Adenosine stimulates nearby granular cells.
  5. Granular cells contract, constricting the afferent arteriole.
  6. GFR falls back to normal.
  7. Mesangial cells may also contract, further limiting GFR.

When GFR falls: the macula densa relaxes the afferent arterioles and mesangial cells, blood flow increases and GFR rises back to normal. This is negative feedback.

1. A drop in blood pressure: baroreceptors in the carotid and aorta stimulate the sympathetic system (also less stretch of the granular cells and less NaCl at the macula densa).
  2. Sympathetic fibres trigger renin release by the granular cells.
  3. Renin converts angiotensinogen (liver; 453 amino acids) into angiotensin I (10 aa).
  4. In the lungs and kidneys, ACE (endothelium) converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II (8 aa).

Angiotensin II, the active hormone that raises BP:

  • Potent vasoconstrictor throughout the body.
  • Constricts the efferent arteriole, raising GFR despite low BP.
  • Lowers pressure in the peritubular capillaries, enhancing NaCl and H2O reabsorption.
  • Stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone (Na+ and H2O reabsorption in DCT and collecting duct).
  • Stimulates Na+ and H2O reabsorption in the PCT.
  • Stimulates the posterior pituitary to secrete ADH.
  • Stimulates thirst.

title: ANP and BNP: the opposite system
subject: subj:physio

body.html:
Stimuli: cardiac distension (atria), sympathetic stimulation, angiotensin II. Effects of ANP (and BNP):

  • Kidneys: afferent dilation, efferent constriction → GFR ↑; less Na+ reabsorption → Na+ excretion ↑ (natriuresis, diuresis).
  • Lower renin and aldosterone; vasodilation.
  • Result: blood volume and blood pressure fall.

Every day the kidneys filter about 180 L of plasma and keep 99 percent of it. Filtration depends on a three-layer barrier that stops cells and proteins, and on a small net pressure of about 10 mmHg. Too much filtration drains the body; too little leaves wastes behind.

About 2 mL/s, 120 mL/min, 170 to 180 L/day, 50 to 60 times the blood volume. Only 1 to 2 L of urine is produced, so 99 percent is reabsorbed.

GFR

Fenestrated endothelium70 to 90 nm pores; excludes blood cells; highly permeable
Basement membraneNegatively charged proteoglycan gel; repels albumin; excludes molecules over 8 nm
Filtration slitsPodocyte pedicels; 30 nm, negatively charged slits

Molecules under about 3 nm pass freely (water, electrolytes, glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, wastes, vitamins). Protein-bound calcium, iron and thyroid hormone do not. Plasma is 7 percent protein; filtrate 0.03 percent.

Damage from infection or trauma causes proteinuria and haematuria; strenuous endurance exercise can do so temporarily through renal hypoxia.

Glomerular hydrostatic pressure favours filtration; colloid osmotic pressure and capsular pressure oppose it. Textbook values: about 60, 32 and 18 mmHg, so net filtration pressure is about 10 mmHg.

GFR = NFP x Kf, where Kf reflects barrier permeability and surface area. High glomerular pressure makes kidneys vulnerable to hypertension: capillary rupture, nephrosclerosis, renal atherosclerosis and renal failure.

Textbook physiology: afferent dilation or efferent constriction raises GFR; afferent constriction lowers it.

GFRResult
Too highFluid passes too fast to reabsorb; urine output rises; dehydration and electrolyte loss
Too lowWastes retained; azotemia

The kidneys do far more than make urine. They filter plasma and excrete wastes, they keep the blood stable (volume, pressure, osmolarity, ions, pH), and they act on the whole body as an endocrine and metabolic organ: erythropoietin, calcitriol and, in starvation, gluconeogenesis.

PartFunction
KidneysUrine formation; retroperitoneal position
UretersTransport urine from kidneys to bladder
BladderStore urine until voided
UrethraCarry urine from the bladder to the outside

The kidneys filter blood plasma, removing metabolic wastes, endogenous hormones, exogenous chemicals (toxic substances, therapeutic medications) and free radicals (detoxification), then excrete them in the urine.

Waste = any substance useless to the body or present in excess; metabolic waste = waste produced by the body. The nitrogenous wastes:

WasteOrigin
UreaProteins → amino acids → NH2 removed → ammonia → the liver converts ammonia to urea
Uric acidCatabolism of nucleic acids
CreatinineCatabolism of creatine phosphate

Found in urineName
AlbuminAlbuminuria
ProteinsProteinuria
GlucoseGlucosuria
KetonesAcetonuria
ErythrocytesHaematuria
LeukocytesPyuria

The kidneys maintain blood homeostasis by regulating:

  • Blood volume and pressure
  • Osmolarity
  • Electrolyte (ion) concentrations
  • Acid-base balance (H+ / HCO3−)

• Erythropoietin (EPO): stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow. In hypoxia (e.g. severe anaemia) the kidneys can raise EPO more than 100-fold. Loop: anaemia → low O2-carrying capacity → less tissue oxygenation → kidney secretes more EPO → more red cells → normal concentration.
  • Oxygen sensing (Nobel Prize 2019): hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) is degraded at normal oxygen tension; in anaemia or hypoxia it persists and promotes EPO, erythropoiesis, angiogenesis (VEGF) and metabolic adaptation.
  • Calcium: the kidneys take part in calcitriol (vitamin D) synthesis; calcitriol raises intestinal calcium absorption (calbindin, VDR). PTH raises renal calcium reabsorption; calcitonin lowers plasma calcium.
  • Gluconeogenesis: in starvation the kidneys synthesise glucose from amino acids (the liver and kidney share gluconeogenesis).
  • They also clear hormones from the blood and detoxify free radicals.

The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney: a glomerulus that filters plasma, then a renal tubule that takes back almost everything useful. Of about 120 mL/min filtered, about 119 mL/min returns to the blood and only about 1 mL/min becomes urine. ADH sets how much water the collecting duct keeps.

• Each kidney has over 1 million nephrons.
  • Physiological nephron loss: about 1% per year from age 30.
  • Each nephron = glomerulus + renal tubule.
SegmentJob
1. GlomerulusFilters small solutes from the blood
2. Proximal convoluted tubuleReabsorbs ions, water, nutrients; removes toxins; adjusts filtrate pH
3. Descending loop of HenleAquaporins let water pass into the interstitial fluid
4. Ascending loop of HenleReabsorbs Na+ and Cl− into the interstitial fluid
5. Distal tubuleSelectively secretes and absorbs ions for blood pH and electrolyte balance
6. Collecting ductReabsorbs solutes and water

• Filtrate collects in the capsular space and flows into the proximal convoluted tubule.
  • Note the vascular and urinary poles; the afferent arteriole is larger than the efferent arteriole.
  • Also called the glomerular capsule (Bowman's capsule).
  • Glomerular capillaries are fenestrated: large amounts of solute-rich fluid pass, but there should not be high amounts of protein in urine.
  • The inner capsule layer has podocytes whose foot processes (pedicels) surround the basement membrane; the clefts between them are filtration slits, where filtrate enters the capsular space.
  • Mesangial cells: smooth muscle-like cells that regulate glomerular blood flow by contracting and engulf macromolecules caught during filtration.

1. Glomerular filtration: creates a plasma-like filtrate.
  2. Tubular reabsorption: removes useful solutes from the filtrate and returns them to the blood.
  3. Tubular secretion: removes additional wastes from the blood and adds them to the filtrate.
  4. Water conservation: removes water from the urine, returns it to the blood, concentrates wastes.

TimeFiltrate (GFR)

Of plasma entering the afferent arteriole, 20% is filtered and 80% goes on to the peritubular capillaries; more than 19% is reabsorbed, so less than 1% is excreted and more than 99% returns to the circulation.

Reabsorption and water conservation = 119 mL/min; urine = 120 − 119 = 1 mL/min (1440 mL/day ≈ 1.5 L/day).

Water loss: urine, sweating, respiration (expiration), faeces (diarrhoea ++), and others: bleeding, vomiting, rhinorrhoea, tears.

ADH (vasopressin), from the posterior pituitary, acts on the collecting duct (aldosterone from the adrenal cortex also retains water with Na+):

  1. Vasopressin binds its membrane receptor.
  2. The receptor activates the cAMP second messenger system (G protein, adenylate cyclase, protein kinase A).
  3. The cell inserts aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water pores into the apical membrane (exocytosis of storage vesicles).
  4. Water is absorbed by osmosis into the blood (300 mOsm filtrate vs 600 to 700 mOsm medullary interstitium; leaves through AQP3 on the basolateral side).
ADHWater reabsorbedUrine
Normal119 mL/min1 mL/min, about 1 500 mL/day
Maximal119.75 mL/min0.25 mL/min, about 375 mL/day
Absent105 mL/min15 mL/min, about 22 500 mL/day

Tubular reabsorption reclaims water and solutes from tubular fluid and returns them to the blood. The proximal tubule takes back about 65%; the descending limb about 20% more; the last 15% is hormone-controlled. The countercurrent multiplier of the loop of Henle builds the salty medulla that lets water leave.

CorticalJuxtamedullary
Share85%15%
LoopShortVery long; maintain the medullary salinity gradient and conserve water
Efferent arterioleBranches into peritubular capillaries around PCT and DCTBranches into vasa recta around the long loop

Juxtamedullary nephrons are better at making concentrated urine. Physiological nephron loss: about 1% per year from age 30.

• Transcellular route: through the cytoplasm of PCT cells and out their base.
  • Paracellular route: between PCT cells; junctions are leaky and let much water through.
  • Reabsorbed fluid is taken up by the peritubular capillaries.
  • Na+–K+ pumps on the basal surface keep Na+ from accumulating: primary active transport (use ATP).
  • Symports on the apical surface: secondary active transport, no direct ATP but depend on the Na+ gradient set by the pumps.
  • Glucose is co-transported with Na+ by SGLT proteins; normally all glucose is reabsorbed.

• Reabsorbs about 65% (2/3) of the glomerular filtrate, and secretes some substances from the blood into the tubular fluid.
  • Prominent microvilli, great length, abundant mitochondria for active transport.
  • PCTs alone use about 6% of resting ATP and calorie consumption.
  • Na+ is actively transported out to set up the gradient that drives osmosis; Cl− follows passively and water follows by osmosis.
  • Fluid leaving is reduced to 1/3 of the original volume but is still isosmotic.

Significance: 65% of salt and water reabsorbed is still too much filtrate left. Another 20% of water is reabsorbed in the descending limb (continuous, unregulated). The final 15% is absorbed later under hormonal control. Fluid entering the loop is isotonic.

Water cannot be pumped and will not cross if isotonic, so the loop builds a concentration gradient; the ascending limb sets it up.

Descending limbAscending limb
Permeable to water, impermeable to solutesPermeable to solutes (active Na+ transport, Cl− follows), impermeable to water

Repeating cycles of pumping and fluid advancing multiply a small difference (300 → 400/200) into a gradient from 300 mOsm in the cortex to about 1 200 to 1 400 mOsm deep in the medulla. 'Countercurrent' = fluid flows in opposite directions in the two adjoining limbs. The kidneys keep plasma osmolarity at 300 mOsm.

Stress runs on two systems. The fast one is nervous: the sympathetic system and adrenal medulla (SN and SAM) produce fight or flight within seconds. The slow one is hormonal: the HPA axis, CRH to ACTH to cortisol. Acute stress protects you; chronic stress damages almost every organ.

SystemEffects
NervousDizziness, headache, pain, anxiety, depression, aggression, cognitive impairment, stroke
CardiovascularCoronary disease, infarction, heart failure, sudden death, dysrhythmias, hypertension
GastrointestinalAcid and pepsin hypersecretion: peptic ulcer, GERD
MusculoskeletalChronic pain, TMJ pain, worse arthritis
RespiratoryAsthma, COPD
ReproductiveAltered sex hormones and menses, infertility, impotence
SkinWorse lesions, rashes, itching, cold skin

Resilience is a dynamic, lifelong process involving active protective biology in the stress systems, neural circuits and immunity, shaped by genes and environment.

TermMeaning
StressorA condition that challenges homeostasis
StressThe physiological or psychological response to a stressor
HardinessCoping with stress and remaining healthy
ResilienceBouncing back from the initial negative effects
EustressStress that enhances function
DistressPersistent stress unresolved by coping

Hans Selye (1936) defined stress as the nonspecific response to any demand: the general adaptation syndrome. His alarm triad: an enlarged adrenal cortex, involution of the thymus, spleen and lymph nodes, and bleeding gastric and duodenal ulcers. Up to 70 percent of primary care visits may relate to stress and lifestyle.

1. Mental: stimulated mental activity.
  2. Adrenal: epinephrine release from the medulla.
  3. Cardiovascular: faster, stronger heart; higher cardiac output and pressure; blood to muscle and heart, away from gut and kidneys.
  4. Metabolic: higher metabolic rate, blood glucose, glycolysis and coagulation.
Adrenal regionHormones
Zona glomerulosaMineralocorticoids (aldosterone)
Zona fasciculataGlucocorticoids and androgens
Zona reticularisAndrogens and glucocorticoids
MedullaEpinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine

The paraventricular nucleus releases CRH, which drives ACTH from the anterior pituitary, which drives cortisol from the adrenal cortex. Cortisol is the main inhibitor of CRH and ACTH.

Cortisol effectDetail
MetabolicAnti-insulin; permissive for glucagon and catecholamines
VascularPermissive for catecholamines (more alpha receptors)
ImmuneAnti-inflammatory
RenalRegulates water excretion

Brain structures: prefrontal cortex; amygdala, hippocampus and hypothalamus; brainstem medulla, locus coeruleus (noradrenaline, arousal) and raphe nuclei (serotonin).

Immunity: glucocorticoids are first anti-inflammatory, then sensitise immunity in recovery; endorphins rise and suppress immunity; growth hormone and prolactin fall.

Termination: cortisol feedback, and the hippocampus-to-PVN circuit, switch the response off; damage to it prolongs stress.

The brain-gut-microbiome axis links stress to gut disease; the gut makes 95 percent of the body's serotonin.
