Response phases: first the rapid SN and SAM; then the sluggish, amplified, protracted HPA.

Acute stress lasts under 2 days to 4 weeks: SN, SAM and HPA rise, the parasympathetic system falls. Chronic stress lasts longer than a month.

Taste and smell are the chemical senses. Taste works through taste buds and five basic qualities; smell works through olfactory neurons in the nose. Together they shape flavour, and their loss harms nutrition. Smell loss can even be an early warning of Parkinson's or Alzheimer's.

Diseases have characteristic smells and tastes, and electronic noses can detect lung cancer or MRSA from breath. In the US, 7 million adults have taste disorders and 14 million smell disorders; 1 to 2 percent have lost smell entirely, rising with age.

TasteExampleSignals
SaltyNaClSodium, osmotic balance
SweetSucroseEnergy
UmamiMSGSavoury, energy-rich food
SourHCl, tartaric acidAcid (aversive)
BitterQuininePossible toxins (aversive)

Responses are innate: newborns react differently to bitter and sweet. Taste buds lie in papillae on the tongue and on the soft palate, larynx, uvula, pharynx, epiglottis and upper oesophagus; each holds about 100 receptor cells.

The chemical must dissolve in saliva and touch the gustatory hairs. Binding depolarises the cell; voltage-gated channels fire; Ca2+ influx releases transmitter.

  • Salty: Na+ through a selective channel (Na+ and Li+ only), blocked by amiloride.
  • Sour: H+ through PKD2L1, a TRP channel.

Coding may be specific or distributed; there is no agreed model. Perception is shaped by smell, temperature, texture and experience.

DisorderMeaning
AgeusiaComplete loss of taste
HypogeusiaReduced taste
HypergeusiaEnhanced taste
ParageusiaDistorted taste
PhantogeusiaPersistent taste with no stimulus

Causes are widespread but uncommon: Addison's disease (salt craving), dental and oral infection, respiratory infection, head trauma, tumours, Bell's palsy, deficiencies, wisdom tooth extraction, MS, cancer, radiation, chemotherapy and drugs.

Olfactory receptor cells are neurons; signals go to the olfactory bulb, the first central relay. Smells habituate rapidly. Some diseases smell: diabetic ketosis of decomposing apples, typhoid of baked bread.

DisorderMeaning
HyposmiaReduced smell
AnosmiaLoss of smell, acquired or congenital
ParosmiaDistorted smell
PhantosmiaSmell without odour
CacosmiaAll odours unpleasant
AgnosiaDetects but cannot classify odours

Ageing lowers sensitivity; neurogenesis falls about 90 percent in old mice, and new bulb neurons come from the subventricular zone via the rostral migratory stream. Smell loss is an early sign of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Only nasal causes are treatable: surgery or corticosteroids.

Two sensors, two kinds of motion. The otolith organs (utricle and saccule) feel gravity and linear acceleration; the semicircular canals feel rotation. Their signals keep you upright and keep your eyes steady while your head moves.

Balance combines vestibular, visual and proprioceptive input, integrated mainly by the cerebellum, below consciousness. Kinesthesis is the somatosensory sense of body-part position; equilibrium is vestibular.

The vestibular apparatus lies in the petrous temporal bone, a bony and a membranous labyrinth, and senses the orientation and motion of the head, relayed by CN VIII to the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum.

Stereocilia sit in a gel: the otolithic membrane (maculae) or the cupula (canals). Apices face endolymph. Bending toward the tallest row opens channels.

Maculae (utricle, saccule)Cristae (canals)
DetectGravity, linear acceleration, pitch and rollAngular acceleration
GelOtolithic membrane with otoconiaCupula
OrientationUtricle horizontal, saccule verticalThree canals at right angles

Rotation: starting, the endolymph lags and tilts the crista opposite to the rotation; stopping, it tilts the same way; at steady speed the cupula returns to rest. Turning right excites the right lateral canal and inhibits the left.

Tilt: otoconia bend the bundles; cells on the upward slope of the striola fire more, those downward less.

title: The vestibular nerve and central pathways
subject: subj:physio

body.html: Bipolar neurons in the vestibular ganglion. The superior division supplies the lateral and anterior cristae and most of the utricle; the inferior division supplies the saccule and the posterior crista via the singular nerve (foramen singulare). The nerve enters at the cerebellopontine angle and ends in the vestibular nuclei, projecting to motor nuclei, the cerebellum and the thalamus, then cortical areas 2v, 3a, 7 and the parieto-insular vestibular cortex.

The MLF links the vestibular nuclei to the nuclei of III, IV and VI and upper spinal motor neurons, keeping gaze fixed. The vestibulo-ocular reflex rotates the eyes opposite to head movement; the flocculus adapts it long term.

ConditionFeatures
NystagmusInvoluntary jerky eye movement from abnormal vestibular input
Caloric testWarm or cold water stimulates the lateral canal crista
Ménière's diseaseHigh spontaneous vestibular firing: dizziness, nausea
Internuclear ophthalmoplegiaMLF lesion: poor ipsilateral adduction, abducting nystagmus; seen in MS

The eye is a camera. The cornea and lens focus light, the iris sets the aperture, and the retina is the film. Most exam questions sit on four ideas: refraction, the pupil reflexes, accommodation, and the retinal cells.

Vision needs an object, light in the purple to red range, and photoreceptors that turn light into action potentials.

Light bends at transparent surfaces, more when refractive indices differ widely and when it strikes off-perpendicular; air's index is 1. Dioptre = 1 / focal length in metres (50 cm = 2 D); convex lenses are positive, concave negative.

There are four refraction points: air-cornea, cornea-aqueous, aqueous-lens, lens-vitreous. The cornea holds two thirds of the eye's refractive power.

Corneal reflex: trigeminal in, facial out, closing the eye and increasing tears.

Miosis in bright light, mydriasis in the dark. A small pupil increases depth of focus and acuity.

Light reflex: optic nerve, pretectal area, Edinger-Westphal nucleus, ciliary ganglion, constrictors (parasympathetic). Dilation in the dark is sympathetic via the cervical ganglion. Because the pathways decussate, light in one eye gives direct and consensual constriction. A lost reflex after head injury suggests brainstem damage.

Aqueous humour is made by the ciliary body, fills the anterior chamber and drains through the canal of Schlemm, feeding the lens and cornea and setting intraocular pressure. Blocked drainage causes glaucoma.

Vitreous humour is a jelly present from birth; it holds the retina against the choroid. Shortened collagen can pull the retina off: retinal detachment, an emergency usually after trauma.

Ciliary muscle contracts: zonules relax, lens thickens, power rises, near vision (parasympathetic). Ciliary muscle relaxes: lens flattens, distant vision. The near response = accommodation + miosis + convergence.

ConditionProblem
PresbyopiaLens stiffens with age; near vision fails
MyopiaFocus in front of the retina
HyperopiaFocus behind the retina
AstigmatismUneven cornea or lens surface; cylindrical lenses

Visual acuity is tested at 20 feet (6 m); normal is 20/20, or 1.

The macula and fovea: 2 percent of the retina, a third of ganglion cells, cone-rich, highest acuity. The optic disc has no photoreceptors: the blind spot. Fundus findings: optic atrophy, papilloedema, macular degeneration.

CellRole

RodsBlack and white, scotopic, peripheral
